title: Govt. signals stronger capital market push in 2027 Budget | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 28 October 2026 00:00
-     - 19

Finance and Planning Deputy Minister Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando 

– Pic by Sameera Wijesingha

Finance and Planning Deputy Minister Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando yesterday said the Government’s capital market policies would be far more visible in the 2027 Budget, conceding that steps taken over the past two years had not been widely seen, leading some to conclude it had done little for the market.

“You will see that visibility in a bigger way in this (2027) Budget,” Dr. Fernando told the Institutional Investor Forum, ‘From Resilience to Sustainable Growth – Industry Forum 2026’, hosted by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka (SEC) and the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE). The Budget proposals will be presented on 12 November, 2026.

He said most of the 12 capital market development proposals submitted by the SEC had already been discussed and accepted by the Finance Ministry. Some will be included in the Budget proposals, while the remainder will be discussed further and implemented in consultation with the CSE and the SEC.

Dr. Fernando said the Government had achieved most of its macroeconomic stabilisation targets ahead of or within the expected timeframe, earning recognition from local stakeholders, diplomatic missions, international agencies and independent rating agencies. The next task, he said, was to move beyond that phase.

“Our challenge is not to live only within stabilisation. We need to move forward from stabilisation to real transformation, where investment is much needed, both local and foreign,” he said.

He identified domestic savings as the immediate opportunity, noting a gap between savings and investment in Sri Lanka, and said the capital market had a critical role in pooling scattered savings and channelling money into the real economy.

To build an environment conducive to investment, the Government will allocate Rs. 2 trillion for capital expenditure, prioritising roads, railways, rural connectivity and networks, logistics, and some social spending. Dr. Fernando, however, conceded that existing bureaucratic systems and resources constrained the State’s ability to spend at speed, and said discussions on accelerating disbursement were already under way.

On fiscal policy, he said revenue mobilisation was well ahead of plan. The original target was to raise Government revenue to 15.4% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by 2030, but the country had already exceeded 16% by end-2025. This year’s target, set under ceilings referenced to the Public Financial Management Act, has been kept at around 15%, which he said could easily be reached.

Once that level is secured, Dr. Fernando said, the Government would have space to fund much-needed public investment and could then consider strategies to reset the present tax structure. He acknowledged issues in corporate income tax and individual income tax, but said rates could not be brought down at this stage without delaying revenue mobilisation. Once revenue reaches the required level, there is a possibility of reducing indirect taxation as well, he said, adding that all tax policy changes would be guided by the principles of fairness, simplicity and convenience.

Turning to State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs), he said only selected entities among the 527 classified as SOEs were engaged in commercial enterprise, with many carrying the label due to legal or other requirements.

“The Government is not interested in engaging in ordinary economic activities such as trading or running a hotel. Our main task is to facilitate,” he said.

Some SOEs will be diversified and others merged, while certain entities, including utilities such as energy, may be retained, either with private sector collaboration or solely with State investment, to prevent market manipulation. A new SOE Act would allow these entities to be reorganised under one umbrella and incorporated as companies with the autonomy to take decisions based on market conditions and risk. Dr. Fernando cautioned that the process would take time.

He also said required legal amendments would be introduced, with new Acts in the pipeline for presentation to Parliament, and that the single window project for investment facilitation through technology was nearing completion.

On monetary conditions, Dr. Fernando said interest rates were relatively high but not volatile, following decisions by the Central Bank to address external sector issues. In the long run, he said, inflation and interest rates must come down.

He flagged the Middle East crisis as an unquantifiable risk, noting that even global experts could not predict its duration or intensity, alongside the escalating global trade war, natural disasters, El Niño and climate change.

Citing the Government’s handling of recent currency pressure as evidence of its commitment to market fundamentals, Dr. Fernando said rumours of bans on motor vehicle and non-essential imports following the Middle East war had fuelled speculation, pushing the import bill up by around $ 2.5 billion a month over three to four months and putting enormous pressure on the currency. The rate prevailing at the time could not be explained by interest rate differentials, he said.

“We did not take unnecessary decisions such as pegging the currency or artificially controlling the market. We let the market run, because we had confidence in our foreign exchange inflows,” he said.

Applying the same principle to equities, he said market distortions arose when prices deviated from fundamentals, often driven by manipulation and information asymmetry, a situation where some participants hold information, including inside information, that others do not. Such practices had fostered a negative public perception of the market and made savers reluctant to invest. Regulators and stakeholders were now working to uphold fundamentals and a level playing field, he said, adding that the Government would not allow private interests to conflict with the public interest.

“We hope that next year, in addition to what we have achieved so far, there will be new developments in the capital market and more foreign investment in the capital market,” Dr. Fernando said.

Central Bank Governor Dr. P. Nandalal Weerasinghe, SEC Chairman Senior Prof. D.B.P.H. Dissabandara and CSE Chairman Dimuthu Abeyesekera also addressed the forum and took part in a panel discussion.

title: Cabinet approves $ 100 m ADB loan to support  Sri Lanka’s economic recovery | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 28 October 2026 00:22
-     - 9

The Cabinet of Ministers has approved a $ 100 million loan agreement with the Asian Development Bank (ADB) to support Sri Lanka’s economic recovery and reform agenda. 

The approval follows the conclusion of formal loan negotiations between the Department of External Resources and the ADB. The proposal was submitted by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in his capacity as Finance, Planning and Economic Development Minister.

“The financing will be provided from the ADB’s regular general capital resources and will consist of two equal components; a policy-based loan of $ 50 million and an investment loan of $ 50 million,” Cabinet Spokesman and Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa said at the weekly post-Cabinet meeting media briefing yesterday.

The facility forms part of the Macro-Recovery Sectoral Development Program, which the Cabinet approved for implementation on 7 September 2026. The program draws on $ 100 million from a broader $ 620 million ADB policy-based loan facility.

The wider facility, approved by the Cabinet on 16 March 2026, covers five sub-programs and is intended to advance Sri Lanka’s reform agenda in line with the IMF’s Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program. The Cabinet had also authorised negotiations with the ADB at that time.

The latest approval comes as the Government considers whether Sri Lanka will require a fresh IMF arrangement after the current EFF program expires in March 2027.

Dr. Jayatissa said the question of a new IMF facility had not been discussed at Monday’s Cabinet meeting. He noted that the evolving international situation, particularly tensions in the Middle East, would influence the Government’s assessment of the economy’s ability to withstand further external shocks without additional support.

“No one can predict what will happen amidst the ongoing Middle East tensions and if the Government is considering a fresh deal with the IMF, it would only be discussed in the early months of 2027,” he said, adding the Government was balancing its growth ambitions against the need to preserve economic stability.

At the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit 2026, President Dissanayake said discussions were underway on the possibility of a new agreement with the IMF that would shift the emphasis from crisis recovery towards economic growth without reversing gains achieved under the existing program. “We are at a mid-level and open about it,” the President said during a fireside chat at the summit, adding that the Government would use the remaining six months of the current arrangement to assess its options before deciding on the future of its engagement with the IMF (https://www.ft.lk/front-page/President-keeps-door-open-to-fresh-IMF-deal/44-798601).

title: Lula seeks deeper Sri Lanka trade ties as $ 1 b target looms | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 28 October 2026 00:21
-     - 14

Anura Kumara Dissanayake (left) with Lula da Silva at the AI Impact 2026 Summit in New Delhi in February 2026

Newly elected for a fourth term, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has expressed hope of deepening bilateral trade and technical cooperation with Sri Lanka, as the two countries work towards elevating bilateral trade to $ 1 billion by 2030.

“I hope we can deepen technical cooperation and bilateral trade between our countries,” Lula said in a post on X, responding to President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s message congratulating him on his election victory. Lula also recalled meeting Dissanayake in India in February this year.

The $ 1 billion trade target was agreed at the Second Round of Bilateral Political Consultations, held in Colombo on 20 March, 2026.

At the talks, both sides acknowledged steady growth in economic cooperation and stressed the importance of broadening engagement in response to evolving global economic dynamics. 

Under the technical cooperation framework, the Dairy Livestock Project and the Sugarcane Project have been finalised and are expected to be signed in the near future, with support from the Brazilian Cooperation Agency (ABC). The parties also committed to finalising outstanding legal instruments on defence, law enforcement, countering human smuggling and transnational organised crime, traditional and Ayurvedic medicine, and diplomatic training.

New avenues for cooperation were identified in agriculture, animal husbandry, agricultural research, ports and shipping, and sports. Both sides agreed to continue close collaboration in bilateral and multilateral forums.

In his post, Lula said Brazilians had shown that democracy could be defended against disinformation and extremism. In an earlier post on X, Dissanayake described Lula’s win as historic, saying it showed that people could not be misled by political dynasties and forces of the past.

“Today, the people of Brazil did not just win an election; they defeated the forces of corruption, division and political lies,” Dissanayake said. 

The target requires roughly a five-fold increase on current levels. Two-way trade was $ 199.5 million in 2025, according to Export Development Board (EDB) data. Sri Lanka’s exports to Brazil fell 13.2% to $ 73.5 million, while imports from Brazil surged 77.5% to $ 126 million, leaving a deficit of $ 52.5 million. Sri Lanka had run a surplus with Brazil every year from 2018 to 2024, according to Sri Lanka Customs data published by the Sri Lankan Embassy in Brasilia.

Exports peaked at $ 84.6 million in 2024, led by apparel, new pneumatic tyres, fuel oil and retreaded or used rubber tyres. Synthetic rubber, sugar and paper were the main imports. The Embassy says there were no recorded significant Brazilian investments in Sri Lanka as of 2023. It lists light vessels, animal feed preparations, rubber gloves, new pneumatic tyres, desiccated coconut, cinnamon and solid or cushion tyres as having strong export potential in Brazil. 

Trade under the Global System of Trade Preferences among Developing Countries (GSTP), to which both countries belong, remains negligible: Sri Lanka’s exports under the scheme were $ 80,000 in 2022.

title: Apparel exports grow in Sept., YTD picture remains cautious: JAAF  | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 28 October 2026 00:20
-     - 6

Sri Lanka’s apparel exports returned to growth in September 2026, an encouraging sign for the sector. Although the nine-month total is still behind last year, the Joint Apparel Association Forum (JAAF) sees the latest result as a positive step.  

Apparel exports for the month came to $ 416.99 million, up 3.47% from $ 403.01 million in September 2025. The United States and the European Union, the sector’s two largest markets, led the gain. Exports to the US grew 7.17% to $ 172.03 million, and exports to the EU (excluding the UK) grew 6.5% to $ 132.46 million. 

Performance across markets was mixed. Exports to the UK fell 5.92% to $ 47.33 million, and exports to other destinations slipped 3.89% to $ 65.17 million. 

The cumulative figures tell a more sobering story. Between January and September 2026, apparel exports totalled $ 3,588.46 million, a decline of 5.52% from $ 3,798.25 million in the same period last year. That is a shortfall of roughly $ 210 million. One strong month, welcome as it is, does not close a gap of that size. 

The decline runs across all major markets over the nine months. The UK saw the steepest fall at 10.85%, followed by the EU at 5.44% and other markets at 5.43%. The US fell 3.69%, the smallest drop among the major markets. 

Changing trade flows of major trading countries, are also shaping the global picture. Chinese apparel shipments to the United States were around 34% lower in the first seven months of 2026, according to US import data. Industry representatives in competing countries note that China and India have been turning more of their attention to Europe following higher US tariffs, which has made the market more price-competitive. 

China’s share of EU apparel imports edged up from 26.9% to 28.6% between January and April 2026. For Sri Lankan manufacturers, this points to a busier European market at a time when overall demand remains soft, and it underlines the importance of competitiveness, reliability and diversification.

JAAF Secretary General Yohan Lawrence said: “September’s growth in the US and EU is encouraging, and it shows our manufacturers can compete when demand is there. We’re still more than five percent behind where we were this time last year. What the industry needs now is steady, competitively priced energy and a supportive policy environment, so that this momentum lasts beyond a single month”.

JAAF sees September as an encouraging sign, particularly with the US and EU both growing, but not yet a turnaround. The industry will be watching closely whether this momentum carries through the remaining months of the year, and whether markets such as the UK can recover.
